CEO and Executive Reputation Management: Protecting the Leader to Protect the Company

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

When investors, journalists or candidates want to understand a company, they increasingly search for the person who runs it. CEO reputation management means controlling what that search shows: identifying risks such as old news, litigation and impersonation, and building a solid, accurate search footprint for the executive before a problem forces the issue.

Why a leader's search results affect the company

For many audiences, the CEO is the company. A bank assessing a credit line, a fund preparing due diligence, a supplier negotiating a large contract or a senior hire weighing an offer will type the leader's name into Google long before they read the annual report. Whatever appears on page one becomes part of their judgement about the business.

In Italy this effect is stronger than many boards expect. Family-owned groups and mid-sized companies are often identified with their founder or managing director, and local press in cities like Milan, Turin or Bari covers business leaders personally. A negative article about the person therefore travels to the brand, while a weak or empty profile leaves room for others to define the narrative. We have looked at the financial side of this in our article on how online reputation affects company value.

Typical risks in executive reputation management

Most executive reputation problems come from a handful of predictable sources, and the majority of them exist long before anyone notices them. A systematic review usually reveals at least one of the following:

  • old news about investigations, inspections or disputes that ended without consequences but still rank for the executive's name;
  • court records, insolvency proceedings or company registry data from a previous role in a business that failed;
  • fake LinkedIn or social profiles used for impersonation, including “CEO fraud” schemes that target employees and suppliers;
  • homonyms, where a namesake with a criminal record or a controversial public life dominates the results;
  • personal details such as home address, family members or private social accounts visible to anyone;
  • critical reviews by former employees on recruiting platforms that mention the leader by name.

The risk is not limited to classic search. Generative answers in Google AI Overviews and chatbots summarise the same sources, so an outdated article can be repeated as current fact in a two-line answer about the executive.

What to check first

Start with the searches that real stakeholders run: the full name, the name with the company, the name with the city, and the name with words such as “indagato”, “truffa” or “fallimento”. Look at Google Images and autocomplete suggestions too, and ask the main AI assistants who the person is. Note every result on page one and the first half of page two, and mark each as owned, neutral, positive or harmful.

Building the executive's search footprint

The most effective protection is a page one filled with accurate, authoritative content that the executive or the company controls. Search engines rank sources they trust, so a leader with a strong professional presence is far harder to damage than one whose name returns only a registry entry and an old news story.

  1. A complete LinkedIn profile in English and Italian, with a consistent headline, a real photo and regular, substantive posts.
  2. A dedicated biography page on the company website, with structured data of type Person linking to official profiles.
  3. A personal website or professional page on the executive's own domain, useful when the name is common or shared with others.
  4. Interviews, podcasts and conference talks with reputable Italian and international outlets, which create independent, credible results.
  5. Bylined articles in trade publications on topics where the executive has real expertise.
  6. Consistent profiles on platforms that rank well for names, such as Crunchbase or speaker pages of industry events.

Consistency matters more than volume. The same name spelling, role, photo and description across all sources helps Google recognise the executive as a single entity, which in turn supports a knowledge panel that can be claimed and corrected.

Dealing with old news, lawsuits and impersonation

Harmful content needs a decision for each item: remove, update, delist, or outrank. An accurate but outdated article about a private investigation that ended in dismissal is a candidate for a request to the publisher and, if needed, for delisting under GDPR art. 17 and the Google Spain ruling (C-131/12). Executives face a stricter balancing test than private individuals because of their public role, so the request must explain why the information is no longer relevant to that role. Our guide to what the right to be forgotten can remove explains where the line usually falls.

Where proceedings ended in acquittal or dismissal, the Riforma Cartabia (art. 64-ter disp. att. c.p.p.) allows the person to obtain a court annotation that supports deindexing. Fake profiles should be reported to the platform as impersonation and, when they are used to defraud staff or partners, to the Polizia Postale. False statements of fact that damage the executive's honour may amount to defamation under art. 595 c.p., but a criminal complaint is a serious step that can attract further coverage and should be weighed with counsel.

For a public company leader, the goal is rarely a perfect page one. It is a page one where the most important facts are accurate, current and told in the executive's own words.

Reputation management for executives as a governance task

The executive's reputation should have an owner inside the company, usually communications together with legal, and a clear process rather than reactions to individual incidents. Without that, problems are discovered by a journalist or an investor instead of the team that could have prepared for them.

Three moments deserve particular attention. Before appointing a new CEO or board member, a discreet search review avoids surprises that would otherwise surface on announcement day. Before a fundraising round, a listing or an acquisition, the leadership team's search results should be checked with the same care as the financial statements. During a crisis, the executive's personal channels need an agreed line so that statements from the company and from the leader do not contradict each other.

Ongoing monitoring closes the loop: alerts on the name, periodic checks of page one and of AI answers, and a quick escalation path when something new appears. The same strong executive presence also supports hiring, as we described in our article on online reputation and employer brand.

Where to start in practice

Begin with an honest picture of what page one shows today, then fix the quick issues and plan the longer work. Correcting an outdated biography, claiming the knowledge panel and completing LinkedIn often change the results within weeks, while delisting requests and new authoritative content take longer to show their effect.

Discretion is part of the job. Executives in Italy are understandably reluctant to involve many people in questions about their past, so the work is best handled by a small team under confidentiality.
